newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO politicians discuss future of Bosnia force.
newsitem.headline: NATO politicians discuss future of Bosnia force.

text.p: The future of the NATO-led peacekeeping operation in Bosnia began to take shape on Monday as officials from the 16-member alliance met to review four possible options for the force.
The North Atlantic Council (NAC) -- NATO's political wing -- was reviewing four options ranging from total withdrawal of troops to leaving the entire near-60,000 force in place.

But the direction the peace Implementation Force for Yugoslavia (IFOR) is most likely to take is centred around two alternatives which favour a gradual reduction in troop strength over the next 12 months.
The first, favoured by NATO's military chiefs, will see IFOR reduced by about half with a substantial "crack force" based locally to prevent and deter any possibility of conflict resuming.

The second, preferred by politicians, calls for a similar reduction but with a rapid reaction force based outside Bosnia. Troops in the country would instead concentrate their efforts on stabilisation and reconstruction.
"The final version will be somewhere between these two," one NATO diplomat told Reuters. "The other options (withdrawal or status quo) are the unlikely versus the undesirable."

The final decision is not the 16-nation NATO's alone to make, however. Officials said all 33 countries contributing to the force will be consulted and a final decision is not expected until later this month.

However, the NAC's deliberations on Monday are likely at least to narrow the choice down. Officials will ask NATO's supreme commander, U.S. General George Joulwan, to prepare a report on what military chiefs believe the best option to be. Joulwan will report back on December 18.
IFOR was set up last year to police the U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accord which brought a fragile truce after years of conflict in the former Yugoslavia.
At its peak it numbered over 60,000 troops from 33 nations and included soldiers from former Cold War enemies working together.
Diplomats said NAC officials were more likely to spend time discussing how long the next phase of IFOR's deployment should be.
Their current mandate is due to expire on December 20 and government leaders from many contributing nations have made no secret of their desire to get out sooner rather than later.
"The U.S. election has lifted a big cloud on the future of the force," said one diplomat, "but it is still important that we let the Bosnians know we do not want to be around forever."
U.S. President Bill Clinton and his Republican election opponent Bob Dole were careful not to make any commitment to the IFOR force during their campaigns for fear of alienating voters.
But NATO diplomats hope that with the security of a further four years in office, Clinton will now be prepared to commit American troops to the next stage of the effort.
"If we don't have a measured, careful, next 12 months all the work of the previous year will be in vain," said one diplomat.
